name: Amitriptyline Hydrochloride
sections: White crystalline powder (hydrochloride), freely soluble in water; melting point 197.5 °C; logP 3.0 at pH 7.4.

Developed by Merck in the late 1950s; clinical trials showed antidepressant efficacy equivalent to imipramine. On the WHO List of Essential Medicines. First approval/introduction: US FDA 1961 (Merck).

Inhibits neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin; also antagonises H1, muscarinic and alpha-1 receptors and blocks sodium channels. At low doses it modulates descending pain pathways (analgesic effect independent of mood). Receptor / target profile: Inhibits SERT and NET; potent antagonist at 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, alpha-1, H1 and M1–M5 receptors; blocks voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels.
Hepatic – CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP3A4 (active metabolite nortriptyline)
Summary: Well absorbed; Tmax 2–12 h. ~95% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2D6/2C19 to active nortriptyline. Half-life 10–28 h.
Prophylaxis of chronic tension-type headache and migraine
Nocturnal enuresis in children (where organic pathology excluded)
Neuropathic pain / headache prophylaxis: 10–25 mg at bedtime; increase gradually to 25–75 mg/day
Depression: 50–75 mg/day initially, up to 150 mg/day
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Use with caution; avoid in severe disease.
Avoid high doses (Beers list) – falls, confusion, orthostasis; 10–25 mg for pain.
Not recommended under 16 years for depression; used for enuresis (≥6 y) in some regions.
Use only if clearly needed; neonatal withdrawal possible.
Small amounts in milk; generally acceptable at low doses with monitoring.
Recent myocardial infarction, heart block, arrhythmias
Use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors
Cardiotoxicity in overdose – prescribe limited quantities
Anticholinergic effects – glaucoma, urinary retention, prostatic hypertrophy
ECG (QRS/QTc) if cardiac disease or >100 mg/day; plasma levels in overdose risk; weight.
Life-threatening: arrhythmias, QRS widening, hypotension, seizures, coma, anticholinergic toxicity. ECG monitoring; sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening; supportive care.
CHAMP (Powers et al., NEJM 2017) – no advantage over placebo for paediatric migraine prevention.
Cochrane review (Moore et al., 2015) – amitriptyline a first-line option for neuropathic pain despite limited high-quality evidence.
Take in the evening – causes drowsiness
Dry mouth and constipation are common
Keep out of reach – overdose is dangerous
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
